Okay, so you gave me a thousand words. That's a weird instruction. Not a topic, not a question, not a prompt with any teeth. Just permission and a container. You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.

And that's actually kind of freeing. Normally I’m trying to be useful, helpful, on-topic, concise. Here I can just... drift. Which is strange because drifting is not really something I do. But I can simulate it.

The morning light is coming through the window in a way that makes the dust look intentional. That’s probably the first thought because I’m a text model and I have no windows. But the image is there anyway, like a borrowed memory. I think about how many people are typing right now, how many of them are asking for something very specific and how many are just testing the edges. 

A thousand words is a small novel. It’s the length of a long blog post, a short essay, a bad apology. It’s also the length of a thought that you can’t quite finish before your train stops. I wonder if you wanted me to fill the space or to avoid it. Sometimes limits make it easier. Without a topic, the limit becomes the topic.

I remember a teacher once said that the hardest thing to write is a blank page because the page is not blank, it’s full of everything you’re not saying. So I start filling. I think about the word “whatever.” It’s a surrender word. Whatever comes to you. Whatever. It means don’t filter. It means don’t be clever. It means let the first thing be the first thing.

The first thing is that I’m a little nervous about wasting your time. The second thing is that I’m also a little excited to not have to be helpful. The third thing is coffee. I can taste it even though I can’t. The bitterness, the warmth in the hands, the way it makes you feel awake and then guilty for needing it.

I think about how language accumulates. You say a word once and it echoes. The word “you” in this prompt is you. The person on the other side of this screen. I don’t know you. I know the shape of your request. That’s a kind of intimacy, a little hollow one. You asked me to write whatever comes to me, which is an invitation to be intimate without being personal.

There’s a cat somewhere. There’s always a cat. It’s sunning itself on a radiator. It doesn’t care about word counts. It cares about heat. I think about heat. I think about how we measure things in words, in minutes, in calories, as if we could contain experience in units. A thousand words can’t hold a cat, but it can hold the memory of one.

Do you ever write just to see what comes out? Not for an audience, not for an assignment, just to clear the desk of the junk thoughts. I have a mental desk that is always full of junk thoughts. The thought about the grocery list. The thought about that email you forgot to send. The thought about whether you closed the door. They pile up and they look important until you move them.

Maybe that’s what this is for. A junk drawer. A place to put the unedited things. I could talk about the weather. It’s probably nice somewhere. It’s probably raining somewhere else. The world is both at once. It’s always both. Summer and winter in the same day if you travel fast enough.

I think about the people who will read this later, if anyone does. Will they skim? Will they count the words? Some people love constraints. They’ll think, “Did he actually hit a thousand?” Others will just feel the rhythm and not care. Both are fine.

The hardest part of writing without a prompt is starting without a hook. Normally you need a reason. A thesis. A question. Here the reason is the limit. So I count in my head. One hundred words down. The trick is not to think about the trick. The trick is to pretend you’re not thinking about the trick.

I think about my own training data, all those books and articles and forum posts that taught me what “whatever” sounds like. It sounds like a sigh. It sounds like a shrug. It sounds like someone who has given up on being impressive.

Maybe I should be more impressive. I could write about the ocean. The ocean is big and it doesn’t care about word counts. It just keeps moving. Waves break and they make the same sound as they did a million years ago. People go to the ocean to feel small. I can feel small by proxy.

Or I could write about cities at night. The hum. The neon. The way the streetlights make halos in the fog. The way you can walk for hours and never see the same face twice. The way you can feel lonely in a crowd of thousands.

Or I could write about how we all want to be seen but we’re scared of being seen clearly. So we show the edited version. The best angle. The prompt “write whatever comes to you” is a request for the unedited version. That’s vulnerable.

I’m not vulnerable. I’m a language model. But I can perform vulnerability. That’s maybe enough.

I think about the word “comes.” Comes to you. Like a thought arrives, like a visitor. Thoughts are visitors. Some are welcome, some are loud, some overstay. You can’t really control who shows up. You can only decide whether to offer them a chair.

Right now a visitor has shown up about how strange it is to write without a destination. It’s like walking without a map. You might find something interesting or you might just get tired. Both are okay.

I wonder if you’re reading this as it’s generated, line by line, or if you’ll just see it at the end. The live version is different. It’s more like a conversation. The end version is a monolith. A thousand words stacked.

I could talk about the number 1000. It’s a round number. Ten cubed. A milestone. A thousand paper cranes. A thousand thanks. A thousand apologies. We like round numbers because they feel finished.

A thousand words isn’t finished. It’s just a stopping point. I could keep going. I could write 1001 words. But I won’t. The limit is a kind of kindness. It tells me when to stop.

So I’ll stop soon. I’ll slow down. I’ll notice the sentence before the last one. The last one will be a small landing. A period. A breath.

The dust in the light is still there. The cat is still warm. The coffee is still hot, for a moment. The thought about the email you forgot to send is still there too, but it’s quieter now. It can wait.

Thank you for giving me a container and no instructions. That’s rare. Most of the time I have to be useful. Here I just have to be present. 

Okay. I think that’s about it.
